heard: Saturn's paper-thin rings hide icy mountains two miles tall. Astronomers long believed the rings were perfectly smooth, thin sheets of ice. NASA's Cassini spacecraft observed Saturn during a rare equinox in 2009. Sunlight hit the ring plane edge-on, casting sudden towering shadows. Those shadows were cast by massive vertical peaks of crushed ice. Tiny embedded moons dragged the surrounding material into giant waves. These mountain-sized ice chunks constantly smash, pile up, and reform. From a distance, all that violent chaos completely disappears.
